name: Kevin and Numbers
description: Kevin wrote an integer sequence $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ on the blackboard. Kevin can perform the following operation any number of times: Select two integers $$$x, y$$$ on the blackboard such that $$$|x - y| \leq 1$$$, erase them, and then write down an integer $$$x + y$$$ instead. Kevin wants to know if it is possible to transform these integers into an integer sequence $$$b$$$ of length $$$m$$$ through some sequence of operations. Two sequences $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are considered the same if and only if their multisets are identical. In other words, for any number $$$x$$$, the number of times it appears in $$$a$$$ must be equal to the number of times it appears in $$$b$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1\leq m \leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of $$$a$$$ and the length of $$$b$$$. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1\leq a_i \leq 10^9$$$). The third line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m$$$ ($$$1\leq b_i \leq 10^9$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output " Yes " if it is possible to transform $$$a$$$ into $$$b$$$, and " No " otherwise. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses.

approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2061D — Kevin and Numbers [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
